about: What the guide says of each public name that the tests and measurements do not produce: what it is for, its security, where the world uses it (each fact with its source) and when to choose it; and the decision table of the chapter "Choose by use case". tools/hash/doc_tables.py renders the comparison tables, the backend lists, the decision table and doc/llms.txt from it, doc/capabilities.json and the measured data; it fails when a function of the capability table has no entry here. Support, size and speed are never written here: they come from the capability table and the measurements.

layout.schema: This description. The version of the layout is "version"; a change of layout raises it.
layout.page: The URL the guide is published at, which doc/llms.txt links.
layout.chapters[]: One per chapter of doc/capabilities.json, in the guide's order: chapter (its key there), title (the chapter's heading), anchor (its id), file (the .adoc that teaches it), summary (one sentence for doc/llms.txt).
layout.functions{}: Per public name of doc/capabilities.json: standard (only where the capability table's algorithm names several standards: this name's own), summary (one sentence), output, security (in plain words, with its source in sources), status (recommended, legacy, broken or not cryptographic), webcrypto (the WebCrypto name, or null when the browser's Web Cryptography API has none), anchor (the guide's section), uses[] ({text, source}: where it is used, each with its source), choose (when to choose it).
layout.use_cases[]: The rows of "Choose by use case": need (I need to ...), use (the function, with its parameters), function (the name in doc/capabilities.json whose backends the row lists), backend (what to do about the backend), example (the program of example/ that shows it) and anchor (the guide's section).

chapters.title: Digests
chapters.summary: Cryptographic hash functions: a fixed-size fingerprint of any data, for integrity, content addressing, identifiers and signatures.

chapters.title: Message authentication
chapters.summary: Keyed hashes: a tag that only the holder of a secret key can compute, so that a receiver knows a message is genuine; and SipHash for hash tables.

chapters.title: Key derivation
chapters.summary: HKDF, PBKDF2 and BLAKE2b subkeys: keys from a shared secret or a master key (HKDF, libsodium's crypto_kdf), or from a password where a standard demands PBKDF2.

chapters.title: Password hashing
chapters.summary: Argon2id and scrypt: slow, memory-hard functions that make every guess of a stolen password database expensive.

chapters.title: Hashes that are not cryptographic
chapters.summary: Fast hashes for hash tables, checksums against accidents and identifiers that no adversary chooses.

md5_128.summary: MD5, a 128-bit digest, broken: kept to read existing data and protocols.
md5_128.security: broken: collisions are found in seconds

uses.text: legacy checksums and old protocols; RFC 6151 retires it for signatures

md5_128.choose: Only to read or check data that already uses it.

sha1_160.summary: SHA-1, a 160-bit digest, broken: kept to read existing data and protocols.

uses.text: Git's original object ids, with collision detection

sha1_160.choose: Only to read or check data that already uses it.

sha2_224.choose: When a standard asks for it; otherwise SHA-256.

sha2_256.summary: SHA-256, the most widely used 256-bit digest.
sha2_256.choose: The default digest: interoperable everywhere, in every browser, fast with hardware support.

sha2_384.summary: SHA-384, SHA-512 cut to 384 bits, immune to length extension.
sha2_384.choose: When a standard asks for 192-bit strength, or a digest that resists length extension within SHA-2.

sha2_512.summary: SHA-512, a 512-bit digest, faster than SHA-256 on 64-bit machines without SHA hardware.
sha2_512.choose: When a standard asks for it, or for a 512-bit digest.

sha2_512_224.summary: SHA-512/224, SHA-512 with other initial values cut to 224 bits.
sha2_512_224.choose: When a standard asks for it.

sha2_512_256.summary: SHA-512/256, SHA-512 with other initial values cut to 256 bits, immune to length extension.
sha2_512_256.choose: A 256-bit SHA-2 digest that resists length extension, fast on 64-bit machines.

sha3_224.choose: When a standard asks for it.

sha3_256.summary: SHA3-256, the SHA-3 standard's 256-bit digest, a design unrelated to SHA-2.
sha3_256.choose: A standard 256-bit digest that is not SHA-2, immune to length extension.

sha3_384.choose: When a standard asks for it.

sha3_512.choose: When a standard asks for it.

shake_128.summary: SHAKE128, an extendable-output function: as many bytes as the caller takes, 128-bit security at most.
shake_128.security: up to 128 bits, and half the output length for collisions
shake_128.choose: To draw a long stream of bytes from one input, at 128-bit security.

shake_256.summary: SHAKE256, an extendable-output function: as many bytes as the caller takes, 256-bit security at most.
shake_256.security: up to 256 bits, and half the output length for collisions
shake_256.choose: To draw a long stream of bytes from one input, at 256-bit security.

keccak_256.summary: Keccak-256 with the original padding, Ethereum's hash; not SHA3-256.

uses.text: Ethereum's addresses, transaction ids and state

keccak_256.choose: For Ethereum and every format that names Keccak-256; never in place of SHA3-256.

blake2b_512.summary: BLAKE2b, a 512-bit digest faster than SHA-2 in software, with a key of up to 64 bytes.
blake2b_512.choose: A fast software digest or keyed hash where SHA-2 has no hardware support.

blake2s_256.summary: BLAKE2s, a 256-bit digest for 32-bit and small machines, with a key of up to 32 bytes.

blake3.summary: BLAKE3, a very fast 256-bit digest with keyed hashing, key derivation and extendable output in one design.

uses.text: the BLAKE3 specification: a Merkle tree, for verified streaming and content addressing

blake3.choose: Large data verified in parts, content addressing, and key derivation from a context string.

ripemd_160.summary: RIPEMD-160, a 160-bit legacy digest, kept for Bitcoin's hash160.
ripemd_160.choose: For Bitcoin's hash160; never in a new design.

siphash_32.summary: HalfSipHash-2-4, a keyed 32-bit hash for hash tables, with an 8-byte key.
siphash_32.security: a 64-bit key; for hash tables only, not a MAC
siphash_32.choose: Hash tables on 32-bit targets whose keys an adversary chooses.

siphash_64.summary: SipHash-2-4, a keyed 64-bit hash for hash tables keyed by untrusted input, with a 16-byte key.
siphash_64.security: a 128-bit key; for hash tables only, not a MAC
siphash_64.choose: Every hash table, set or Bloom filter whose keys come from the network or another user.

hmac.summary: hmac<H>, HMAC over any Boost.Hash2 hash.
hmac.security: that of H's digest, with a key as long as it
hmac.choose: HMAC over a hash that has no alias of its own.

hmac_md5_128.security: still unforgeable as HMAC, but on a broken hash: legacy

hmac_sha1_160.security: still unforgeable as HMAC, but on a broken hash: legacy
hmac_sha1_160.choose: Only for an existing protocol, such as authenticator-app codes.

hmac_sha2_224.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha2_256.summary: HMAC over SHA-256, the default MAC.
hmac_sha2_256.choose: The default MAC: interoperable, in every browser.

hmac_sha2_384.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha2_512.choose: When a standard asks for it, or for a 512-bit tag.

hmac_sha2_512_224.choose: When a standard asks for it.

uses.text: FIPS 180-4's truncated SHA-512; not libsodium's crypto_auth, which truncates HMAC-SHA-512's tag

hmac_sha2_512_256.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha3_224.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha3_256.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha3_384.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_sha3_512.choose: When a standard asks for it.

hmac_blake2b_512.summary: HMAC over BLAKE2b; a keyed BLAKE2b does the same job faster.

uses.text: RFC 7693, whose keyed mode makes HMAC unnecessary

hmac_blake2b_512.choose: When a protocol names HMAC-BLAKE2b; otherwise a keyed blake2b_512.

fnv1a_32.summary: FNV-1a with a 32-bit result: tiny and simple, not cryptographic.
fnv1a_32.security: none: an adversary finds collisions at will

uses.text: the IETF draft that specifies it

fnv1a_32.choose: Small tables and identifiers no adversary chooses.

fnv1a_64.summary: FNV-1a with a 64-bit result: tiny and simple, not cryptographic.
fnv1a_64.security: none: an adversary finds collisions at will

uses.text: the IETF draft that specifies it

fnv1a_64.choose: Tables and identifiers no adversary chooses.

xxhash_32.summary: xxHash32: a very fast 32-bit checksum, not cryptographic.
xxhash_32.choose: Fast checksums against accidents on 32-bit targets.

xxhash_64.summary: XXH64: a very fast 64-bit checksum, not cryptographic.
xxhash_64.choose: Fast checksums against accidents, as Zstandard's.

xxh3_128.summary: XXH3 with a 128-bit result: a fast checksum, not cryptographic.
xxh3_128.choose: Checksums and identifiers of large data no adversary chooses.

murmur3_32.summary: MurmurHash3 x86_32, a fast 32-bit hash, not cryptographic.
murmur3_32.choose: To match existing data that uses it.

murmur3_128.summary: MurmurHash3 x64_128, a fast 128-bit hash, not cryptographic.
murmur3_128.choose: To match existing data that uses it.

spooky2_128.summary: SpookyHash V2, a fast 128-bit hash, not cryptographic.
spooky2_128.choose: To match existing data that uses it.

hkdf_extract.summary: HKDF-Extract: a uniform pseudorandom key from a secret that is not uniform, such as a Diffie-Hellman result.
hkdf_extract.security: that of the hmac, given input with enough entropy
hkdf_extract.choose: When a protocol names the extract step alone.

hkdf_expand.summary: HKDF-Expand: many keys, each for one purpose, from one pseudorandom key.
hkdf_expand.choose: Keys from a key that is already uniform (a master key), one per info label.

hkdf.summary: HKDF, extract then expand: keys from a shared secret, each separated by its info label.
hkdf.security: that of the hmac, given input with enough entropy
hkdf.choose: The default way to turn one secret into several keys. Never for passwords.

pbkdf2.summary: PBKDF2: a key from a password by many iterations of an hmac; not memory-hard.
pbkdf2.security: each guess costs the iterations; no defence against GPUs beyond that

uses.text: OWASP: 600,000 iterations of HMAC-SHA-256 for passwords

pbkdf2.choose: When a standard or FIPS 140 demands it; otherwise Argon2id for passwords.

blake2b_subkey.summary: BLAKE2b subkeys, libsodium's crypto_kdf: many keys of 16 to 64 bytes from one 32-byte master key, each named by a 64-bit id and an 8-byte context.
blake2b_subkey.security: that of the master key, which must be 32 uniformly random bytes; at most the subkey's length
blake2b_subkey.choose: To derive the keys a libsodium program derives from the same master key, or keys numbered by id from one random master key; hkdf for a secret that is not uniformly random.

argon2id.summary: Argon2id: the recommended password hash, memory-hard, winner of the Password Hashing Competition.
argon2id.security: each guess costs its memory and passes, on a GPU too

uses.text: OWASP's first choice for password storage
Bitwarden's vault key, as an option

argon2id.choose: Storing passwords and deriving keys from them.

scrypt.summary: scrypt: a memory-hard password hash, older than Argon2id.
scrypt.security: each guess costs 128 r N bytes of memory

uses.text: OWASP: N 2^17, r 8, p 1 when Argon2id is not available

scrypt.choose: When a format demands scrypt; otherwise Argon2id.
